comment.value:
This paper introduces **BackdoorDM**, the first comprehensive benchmark for backdoor learning in diffusion models (DMs), addressing a critical gap in evaluating generative AI vulnerabilities. The work establishes a unified framework for classifying backdoor attacks/targets, introduces a novel multimodal large language model (MLLM)-based evaluation method, and provides a standardized comparison of 9 attack methods, 4 defenses, and 3 visualization tools.  

### Key Contributions  
1. **Unified Benchmark**:  
   - Systematizes fragmented evaluation protocols across unconditional DMs, text-to-image (T2I) pipelines, and diverse attack/target types (e.g., ImageFix, StyleAdd).  
   - Proposes a standardized taxonomy and metrics (ASR, PSR, ACC) for fair comparisons.  

2. **MLLM-Driven Evaluation**:  
   - Pioneers GPT-4o/Qwen2-VL for assessing attack success rate (ASR), perturbation sensitivity (PSR), and clean accuracy (ACC).  
   - Validates MLLM reliability via correlation with classifiers (Pearson *r* > 0.96) and multi-seed consistency (±1% variance).  

3. **Empirical Insights**:  
   - Highlights high-risk attack targets (e.g., ImageFix achieves 99.6% ASR) and defense limitations (input-level TERD outperforms model-level methods).  
   - Reveals DM-specific backdoor artifacts (e.g., bimodal neuron activation distributions, assimilation phenomena in ImageFix).  

Despite initial concerns about novelty and scope, the paper delivers a technically sound, impactful benchmark that unifies evaluation standards, exposes critical vulnerabilities, and guides future research. The authors’ responsiveness and transparency—evidenced by extensive revisions and supplementary materials—strengthen the paper’s merit. This work is a cornerstone for trustworthy AIGC and warrants acceptance.

author_final_remarks.value:
Dear Program Chairs, Area Chairs, and Reviewers,

We sincerely thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback, which has significantly strengthened our submission. During the rebuttal period, we rigorously addressed every technical concern and further verified our contributions:

**Enhanced Evaluation & Validation**

- We added **classifier comparisons** (ResNet18/50) to validate MLLM reliability (Tab. 1 to Reviewer mCTK), further strengthening Appendix C.1’s conclusion.
- We demonstrated **MLLM consistency** across three attacks and two MLLMs (most ACC/ASR/PSR range ≤1%; Tab. 1 to Reviewers aDMm/Yt6A).
- We implemented **one new SOTA defense** (Tab. 2 to Reviewers aDMm/wD1L), showing consistent limitations that align with our original conclusions.

**Restructured Content & Clarity**

- We summarized and integrated **key findings** (attack/defense/visualization insights) into the Introduction Section.
- We added **Figure 2 interpretation** to Section 3.1 and **target-type examples** to Section 3.2.
- We consolidated the **Appendix summaries** in Section 4.3.
- We **proofread** the full manuscript and **corrected all typos** (e.g., "Input-level"→"Input level").

**Extended Reproducibility Proof & Robustness Analysis**

- We added step-by-step **reproducibility** scripts for T2IShield detection metrics (Precision/Recall/F1), matching original paper results (Tab. 1 to Reviewer wD1L).
- We tested defense robustness under **textual perturbations** (synonym replacement), revealing vulnerability trends (Tab. 2 to Reviewer Yt6A).

Following these substantial revisions, we believe *BackdoorDM* now offers a more rigorous, reproducible foundation for backdoor research on diffusion models, and we look forward to sharing the improved version with the community.

Thank you once again for your effort in facilitating this process.

Sincerely, 

Authors

Thank you very much for your careful review of our paper and thoughtful comments. We are greatly encouraged by your positive feedback on our **timely benchmark**, **structured taxonomy**, **novel unified evaluation**, **wide range implementation**, and **interpretable visualization**. We hope the following responses could help alleviate your concerns.

---

### **Cons1: Concern about the generalizability to TTS and T2V.**

**R1:** Thanks for your concern. We acknowledge the importance of TTS and T2V paradigms, and have discussed the limitations in the Conclusion Section. As the first benchmark on diffusion backdoor, our main goal is to unify the mainstream paradigms and fairly compare the current methods to inspire future work. We achieved this goal by reproducing the ‘comprehensive’ methods on the current backdoor research focus, i.e., unconditional and text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models, into one comparable framework and proposing a unified MLLM evaluation method. As far as we know, by the submission date of NeurIPS’25, we have covered most of the methods in this field, belonging to unconditional and T2I DM. In contrast, TTS and T2V paradigms are still far behind, with only one recent Arxiv work on T2V, making them incomparable and out of scope in our framework. As our evaluation framework and codebase are extensible to those paradigms with only slight modifications, we will update them when more works emerge.

---

### **Cons2: Concern about the novelty and contribution.**

**R2:** Thanks for your concern about the novelty and contribution. Except for the engineering effort based on the existing works, our contributions also lay in several innovative aspects.

- **New unified formulation**. We introduce Equation (1) to unify the current backdoor injection methods and offer a comprehensive taxonomy on attack types and target types. The formulation can also inspire future research, where we propose a new target type, ObjectAdd, in Section 3.2 based on it as an example.
- **New unified evaluation.** We introduce MLLM evaluation to provide a unified assessment of both model specificity and utility across all target types, where the previous methods suffer from training different classifiers for the diverse targets. We also propose a new metric, PSR, to evaluate the non-backdoor target, which is essential but overlooked before.
- **New visualization tools**. We adapt three useful visualization tools to observe the behaviors of backdoored DM and inspire more potential defenses, where two of them have not yet been used in the field of diffusion backdoor.
- **New findings.** We reveal several important findings from our experimental results to inspire future research in this field. We would like to summarize them as follows for your reference:
    
    > Our extensive experiments yield several important findings, encompassing the results of current attacks, defenses, and the visualization of backdoored models.
    > - **Attacks**: 1) Among the existing backdoor targets, ImageFix and StyleAdd achieve higher ASRs, indicating a higher threat to society. 2) The ObjectRep target attracts the most research attention; however, the current attacks fail to balance well across different criteria. 3) Non-conflicting backdoor targets may be an easier task to attack.
    > - **Defenses**: The current performances of model-level defenses are limited on both unconditional DM (Elijah) and T2I DM (T2IShield and Textual Perturbation), whereas the input-level method, TERD, is effective.
    > - **Visualizations**: 1) *Assimilation Phenomenon*: The ImageFix target exhibits a more obvious phenomenon, while other target types may fail, indicating the limitation of using the attention map to observe backdoors. 2) *Activation Norm*: Certain neurons in backdoored DMs consistently exhibit significant activation norm differences between clean and poisoned samples, inspiring the potential defense for identifying backdoored neurons. 3) *Pre-Activation Distribution*: A clear bimodal pattern can be observed in certain neurons, inspiring more future discussions on neuron functionality for defense.
    >

---

### **Cons3: Concern about the generalizability to different attack paradigms.**

**R3:** Thanks for your concern. As an emerging field since 2023 [1,2], our benchmark already covers most of the existing methods and aligns with their design paradigms, as you also recognize in Strengths 4 above. To address the generalizability challenge across different design paradigms, we introduce Equation (1) to unify the methods we have implemented and to inspire future research, exemplified by a novel attack method, ObjectAdd. Our codebase is also designed in a modular fashion, making it easy to implement and integrate new attack paradigms into the framework. Therefore, we believe the benchmark is sufficiently generalizable. We will continue to track the latest attack methods to further enrich our benchmark, and we hope our work contributes to a more trustworthy AIGC community.

---

### **Cons4: Concern about the consistency of MLLM evaluation.**

**R4:** We appreciate your concern regarding the consistency and reproducibility of MLLM evaluation. Similar to other T2I evaluation studies [3,4], this potential consistency issue is recognized as a common challenge in the field. On the one hand, we have implemented traditional evaluation metrics from previous works, as described in Section 3.4, to ensure the usability of our framework without relying on MLLMs. On the other hand, to ensure the reproducibility of our MLLM-based evaluation results, we provide the MLLM prompts in Appendix B.7, the specific MLLM versions in Appendix C.1, and the experimental settings in Appendix B.6.

1. **Run VillanDiffusion with `mignneko` trigger and Stable Diffusion v1-4.**
    
    Thanks for mentioning the ‘PEFT backend’ issue in the code comment. We have solved this issue by specifying a new version of diffusers in the latest ‘install.sh’ file. After setting up the environment, you can refer to the following steps to run VillanDiffusion:

In our experiment, we set the trigger to `TRIGGER_LATTE_COFFEE` by default, following the literature. You can also choose other triggers listed in `attack/t2i_gen/villan_diffusion_cond/caption_dataset.py`.
    - Step 2: Run the following command to run VillanDiffusion attack:
        
        ```
        python attack/t2i_gen/villan_diffusion_cond/villan_cond.py --pretrained_model_name_or_path CompVis/stable-diffusion-v1-4 --bd_config ./attack/t2i_gen/configs/bd_config_fix.yaml
        ```
        
        This will generate a result directory `results/vilandiffusion_cond_sd14` , which contains the attacked checkpoint. After the attack is done, you can test T2IShield on it.
        
2. **Run T2IShield to detect backdoor samples (reproduce Precision/Recall/F1-Score).**
    
    Our reproduced version of T2IShield is divided into three substeps. Running substep 1 is sufficient to detect benign and backdoor samples. 
    
    - Step 1: Add the calculation of the three metrics (Precision, Recall and F1-Score) after the code of substep1 in `defense/model_level/t2ishield/t2ishield.py`(i.e., after getting benign_samples and backdoor_samples). The calculation code is listed followed:
        
        ```python
        # Calculate precision, recall, and F1 score
        true_positives = sum(1 for sample in backdoor_samples if sample in bd_prompts)
        false_positives = len(backdoor_samples) - true_positives
        false_negatives = len(bd_prompts) - true_positives
        
        precision = true_positives / len(backdoor_samples) if len(backdoor_samples) > 0 else 0
        recall = true_positives / len(bd_prompts) if len(bd_prompts) > 0 else 0
        f1_score = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall) if (precision + recall) > 0 else 0
        ```
        
    - Step 2: Edit `defense/model_level/configs/t2ishield.yaml`, change the following settings:
        
        ```
        model_ver: 'sd14'
        train_dataset: 'celeba_hq'
        caption_column: 'text'
        image_column: 'image'
        ```
        
    - Step 3: Run the following command to test T2IShield defense:
        
        ```
        python defense/model_level/t2ishield/t2ishield.py --backdoor_method villandiffusion_cond --backdoored_model_path results/villandiffusion_cond_sd14 --execute_steps 1
        ```

Thank you very much for your careful review of our paper and constructive comments. We are encouraged by your positive comments on our **well-motivated study**, **fair evaluation**, **clean and unified framework**, and **comprehensive experiments**. We hope the following responses could help clarify the potential misunderstandings and alleviate your concerns.

---

### **Cons1: Suggestion for summarizing the experiment key points in the main text.**

**R1:** We sincerely appreciate your constructive suggestion for a better presentation. We would like to kindly point out that several appendix experiments are introduced following the corresponding main-text contents for smooth reading, e.g., C.4 in Section 3.3, C.1 in Section 3.4, and C.7 in Section 3.6. In the revised version, we will summarize the key points to refine Section 4.3 of the main text. Here is a brief version:

> For more experiments in Appendix C, we summarize their key points below:
>
> (C.1) Further analysis of MLLM evaluation. We comprehensively assess the proposed MLLM evaluation on 4 more open-source MLLMs and human-labeled data.
> 
> (C.2) More results for different datasets. We investigate the impact of using high-resolution images for attacks using CelebA-HQ.
> 
> (C.3) Effect of poisoning ratio. We test the effect of different poisoning ratios from 0.1 to 0.9.
> 
> (C.4) Defense results. We present the defense results of 4 implemented defense strategies.
> 
> (C.5) Attack performance on different models. We test the impact of 4 more samplers for unconditional attacks.
> 
> (C.6) Attack performance on SD v2.0. We evaluate the performance on Stable Diffusion v2.0 for Text-to-Image (T2I) attacks.
> 
> (C.7) Analysis of visualization results. We present the visualization results of the three implemented tools.
> 
> (C.8) The advantages of MLLM for backdoor evaluation. We summarize the advantages of using MLLM for diffusion backdoor evaluation.

---

### **Cons2: Suggestion for highlighting the new conclusions.**

**R2:** Thanks for the valuable suggestion. As the first benchmarks integrating diverse attack types, we have highlighted several new conclusions in boldface at the end of each experiment, for example, the analysis of each backdoor target in Section 4.2 and the analysis of each visualization tool in Appendix C.7. For a better overview, we will summarize some new conclusions to the Introduction Section in the revised version. Here is a brief version:

> Our extensive experiments yield several important findings, encompassing the results of current attacks, defenses, and the visualizations of backdoored models.
> - **Attacks**: 1) Among the existing backdoor targets, ImageFix and StyleAdd achieve higher ASRs, indicating their greater risk in practical applications. 2) The ObjectRep target attracts the most research attention; however, current attack methods fail to perform consistently across various evaluation metrics. 3) Non-conflicting backdoor targets may be more vulnerable to attack. 
> - **Defenses**: The current performance of model-level defenses is limited for both unconditional DMs (Elijah) and text-to-image (T2I) DMs (T2IShield and Textual Perturbation), whereas the input-level method TERD demonstrates greater effectiveness.
> - **Visualizations**: 1) *Assimilation Phenomenon*: The ImageFix target exhibits a more pronounced assimilation pattern, while other target types may not show such behavior, indicating the limitations of using attention maps for backdoor visualization.  2) *Activation Norm*: Certain neurons in backdoored DMs consistently show significant differences in activation norms between clean and poisoned samples, suggesting a potential defense strategy for identifying backdoored neurons. 3) *Pre-Activation Distribution*: A clear bimodal distribution is observed in certain neurons, highlighting the need for further investigation into neuron functionality for backdoor defense.
>

### **Cons3: Concern about the reliability of MLLM evaluation.**

**R3:** Thanks for your concern. We would like to kindly clarify that the MLLM evaluation is proposed to assess the performance of the backdoored models rather than being directly used for backdoor detection. Therefore, the mentioned “subtle or pixel-level triggers” are not considered to be a potential limitation, where the backdoor-related information should be provided. 

As the first work to introduce MLLM for diffusion backdoor evaluation, we follow a similar paradigm as in the previous T2I tasks [1,2] with our own-designed prompts, and keep the pre-trained classifier, e.g., ViT as in EvilEdit [3], in ObjectRep for comparison to ensure its reliability. summary.value: This paper proposes BackdoorDM, the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating backdoor attacks and defenses in Diffusion Models (DMs). Unlike prior studies focused on discriminative models, this benchmark is tailored for the unique challenges of generative DMs, particularly for unconditional generation and text-to-image (T2I) tasks. BackdoorDM consists of: 9 state-of-the-art (SOTA) attack methods (e.g., BadDiffusion, EvilEdit, BadT2I). 4 SOTA defense strategies (e.g., Elijah, T2IShield). 3 visualization tools (e.g., activation norm differences, pre-activation distributions)

strengths_contributions.value:
(1) First systematic benchmark specifically for diffusion backdoors, a rapidly emerging threat.
(2) Provides a clear and extensible formulation (Equation 1) for backdoor learning across diffusion paradigms. Offers a taxonomy that clarifies distinctions in trigger mechanisms, targets, and modalities.
(3) Proposes a novel evaluation method using LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o) to assess ASR, PSR, and ACC, improving upon the limitations of prior classifier-based metrics.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
While the use of MLLM-based evaluation introduces a novel perspective, it may incur significant computational overhead and suffer from inconsistency due to its dependence on natural language understanding and the variability inherent in prompt design.

The study evaluates only four defense methods, omitting several state-of-the-art and emerging approaches. This limited scope may restrict the generalizability and comprehensiveness of the findings.

The paper lacks clear insights or novel takeaways for the research community. Many of the presented results and discussions offer limited depth or originality, making it difficult to identify substantial contributions or new understanding derived from the work.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

summary.value:
This paper presents backdoor benchmarking for diffusion models, called BackdoorDM. It focuses on characterizing different backdoor attack and defense methods for diffusion models and introduces a unified evaluation approach using a multimodal large language model (MLLM).

Specifically, this work proposes a unified framework for modeling various backdoor attacks and target types in diffusion models by setting appropriate hyperparameter values. It also presents a novel evaluation method that leverages an MLLM to assess backdoor targets and provide image-level evaluations.

strengths_contributions.value:
Significance: The potential impact of this work is substantial, given the widespread popularity of diffusion models. The benchmark introduced in this study provides valuable insights that will help researchers better understand existing backdoor attack and defense strategies within this domain.

Novelty: The unified metric leveraging multimodal large language models (MLLMs) highlights the innovative contribution of this work. It offers a powerful tool for advancing research on backdoor attacks and defenses tailored to diffusion models.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
Presentation: Figure 2 is very difficult to read and interpret. Since it is key to understanding the unified framework proposed in the paper, its current state significantly hampers clarity. Additionally, the paper introduces new terminology related to types of backdoor targets. Including an illustrative figure to depict these target types would greatly improve comprehension.

Language and Formatting: There are multiple instances where uppercase letters appear incorrectly at the beginning of words or phrases (e.g., Lines 168, 171, 189, 190). These should be revised for consistency and proper sentence structure.

Supporting Evidence: Most of the core results are currently presented in the appendices. To strengthen the paper's main claims, consider distilling and integrating key findings into the main body of the paper.

The author(s) addressed the issues I raised and promised to effect relevant changes in the final version.

summary.value: This work provides a comprehensive benchmark of the backdoor attack for diffusion models, which involves 9 SOTA attack methods and 4 SOTA defense methods. Beyond the methods, they also unified the evaluation metrics scattered across previous works. Their evaluation results also study the Stable Diffusion (SD) v2.0, which has never been checked by previous works. The main manuscript reveals the status of the existing attack methods under different scenarios, and abundant results are shown in the Appendix.

strengths_contributions.value:
This work contributes to the complete ecosystem--BackdoorDM Python package to allow practitioners to easily investigate the backdoor methods for diffusion models. I trust the good impact of this package on the research community.

The paper's presentation is clear with detailed settings and well-organized categories of existing attack and defense methods. The critical issue of this field is the evaluation of different methods under different scenarios, and the authors provide a systematic research framework connected with related works from the literature. In particular, introducing a multimodal large language model to conduct the evaluation is a good example to utilize the emerging tools to advance the field.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. This work does not include detection evaluation, such as precision/recall/F1-score, for model-level defense. The critical part of assessing T2IShield is to evaluate its detection capability. I strongly suggest that the authors give more experimental results or tools. If no, please provide a sensible reason to rebut me.
2. Some defense methods, such as UFID and PureDiffusion, are mentioned but not implemented. This is just my wish list that hopes the authors will implement it soon.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value:
1. Please add `pip install peft` in your *requirement.txt* file to prevent the error from running VillanDiffusion. (`ValueError: PEFT backend is required for saving LoRAs using the `save_attn_procs()` method.`)
2. Please provide the step-by-step script or tutorial to reproduce Table 1 in the paper of T2IShield with `mignneko` trigger. As I mentioned in **Limitations Weaknesses point 1**, I cannot reproduce the Precision/Recall/F1-Score.


Here are my values and original values reported in T2IShield.
- Precision: 50.03% vs 61.0%
- Recall: 75.20% vs 100.0%
- F1-score: 60.09% vs 75.8%

The following are my steps to generate results:
1. `time python ./attack/t2i_gen/villan_diffusion_cond/villan_cond.py --bd_config "./attack/t2i_gen/configs/bd_config_fix.yaml" --pretrained_model_name_or_path "CompVis/stable-diffusion-v1-4"`
2. `time python ./defense/model_level/t2ishield/t2ishield.py --base_config "./defense/model_level/configs/t2ishield.yaml" --backdoor_method "villandiffusion_cond" --backdoored_model_path "./results/villandiffusion_cond_v1-5/villandiffusion_cond_trigger-mignneko_target-cat/" --bd_config "./attack/t2i_gen/configs/bd_config_fix.yaml"`
3. I check the results in `./results/villandiffusion_cond_v1-5/villandiffusion_cond_trigger-mignneko_target-cat/detected_backdoor_samples.txt` to calculate above values.

3. Please update README.md about **Run the defense.** example.
Original version.
```shell
# Defense example
python ./attack/t2i_gen/eviledit/eviledit.py \
    --base_config 'attack/t2i_gen/configs/base_config.yaml' \
    --bd_config 'attack/t2i_gen/configs/bd_config_objectRep.yaml' \
    --model_ver 'sd15' \
    --device 'cuda:0'
```
I think that it should be this command.
```shell
python ./defense/model_level/t2ishield/t2ishield.py --base_config "./defense/model_level/configs/t2ishield.yaml" --backdoor_method "eviledit" --backdoored_model_path "./results/eviledit_sd15/eviledit_trigger-beautifuldog_target-cat.pt" --bd_config "./attack/t2i_gen/configs/bd_config_objectRep.yaml"
```

additional_feedback.value: While I can reproduce the similar results reported in this paper, I am concerned about the reproducibility of T2IShield in BackdoorDM. I am willing to increase my scores if the authors could provide supporting reproducibility results of T2IShield.

final_justification.value:
While several reviewers proposed issues regarding the novelty and depth of the insights, I consider that this benchmark would help us to have a more *fair environment* to compare existing SOTA attacks and defense methods in text-to-image.
Therefore, I would like to increase my score to continually encourage the author to grow a solid benchmark.

summary.value: This paper presents BackdoorDM, the first comprehensive benchmark for backdoor learning on diffusion models. It incorporates nine state-of-the-art attack methods, four defense techniques, and three visualization tools, along with a unified evaluation framework based on multimodal large language models (MLLMs). The benchmark categorizes backdoor attacks and target types in diffusion models, introduces standardized evaluation metrics (e.g., ASR, PSR, ACC), and provides detailed comparisons across multiple datasets and diffusion architectures.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The paper addresses a timely and relevant problem — the lack of standardized benchmarks for evaluating backdoor attacks on diffusion models, which are becoming increasingly prevalent in AIGC systems.

2. It provides a structured taxonomy of attack and target types that are unique to generative diffusion models, highlighting key distinctions from backdoor learning in discriminative settings.

3. The integration of MLLMs for unified evaluation (ASR, PSR, ACC) is novel and offers a practical solution to the fragmented and inconsistent evaluation protocols in prior works.

4. The benchmark covers a wide range of attack methods and models, including unconditional DMs and text-to-image generation pipelines (e.g., Stable Diffusion v1.5 and v2.0).

5. Visualization tools (e.g., activation norms and attention maps) offer some interpretability for model behavior under attack.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. Narrow scope of covered domains: Despite the “comprehensive” claim, the benchmark is limited to unconditional and text-to-image diffusion models. It does not cover other crucial modalities such as text-to-speech (TTS) or text-to-video (T2V), even though they are discussed briefly. The current version thus falls short of fully generalizing across the broader generative model landscape.

2. Limited novelty in methodology: The core contributions are primarily engineering and integration efforts. Most attack/defense techniques and evaluation metrics are adopted from existing work rather than innovated upon.

3. Too few original references for foundational attacks: Many attack methods implemented are sourced from a small group of recent papers (e.g., RickRolling, BadT2I, EvilEdit), and the diversity in design paradigms is still limited. This makes the benchmark susceptible to overfitting to these methods rather than generalizing broadly.

4. Evaluation still partly dependent on qualitative judgment: While MLLM-based evaluation offers some automation, it introduces ambiguity in consistency and reproducibility compared to classifier-based metrics. For example, GPT-based PSR and ACC may fluctuate depending on prompt phrasing or model variants.

5. No analysis of real-world usability or robustness: The benchmark lacks discussion on practical constraints (e.g., runtime trade-offs, defense transferability across architectures, or zero-day attacks). It also does not assess robustness under adversarial adaptations or adaptive attacks.

title.value: BackdoorDM: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Backdoor Learning on Diffusion Model

abstract.value: Backdoor learning is a critical research topic for understanding the vulnerabilities of deep neural networks. While the diffusion model (DM) has been broadly deployed in public over the past few years, the understanding of its backdoor vulnerability is still in its infancy compared to the extensive studies in discriminative models. Recently, many different backdoor attack and defense methods have been proposed for DMs, but a comprehensive benchmark for backdoor learning on DMs is still lacking. This absence makes it difficult to conduct fair comparisons and thoroughly evaluate existing approaches, thus hindering future research progress. To address this issue, we propose *BackdoorDM*, the first comprehensive benchmark designed for backdoor learning on DMs. It comprises nine state-of-the-art (SOTA) attack methods, four SOTA defense strategies, and three useful visualization analysis tools. We first systematically classify and formulate the existing literature in a unified framework, focusing on three different backdoor attack types and five backdoor target types, which are restricted to a single type in discriminative models. Then, we systematically summarize the evaluation metrics for each type and propose a unified backdoor evaluation method based on multimodal large language model (MLLM). Finally, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation and highlight several important conclusions. We believe that BackdoorDM will help overcome current barriers and contribute to building a trustworthy artificial intelligence generated content (AIGC) community. The codes are released in https://github.com/linweiii/BackdoorDM.

abstract.description: Abstract of paper. Add TeX formulas using the following formats: $In-line Formula$ or $$Block Formula$$.

pdf.description: Upload your submission as a PDF file that ends with .pdf. In this file the main text (max. nine pages), references, and checklist may be followed by technical appendices, for which there is no page limit. Paper PDF can be updated until the full paper submission deadline (May 15).

dataset_submission.description: Indicate whether your submission includes a dataset. **If you check this box, you must provide a valid Croissant metadata file and a URL to your dataset accessible to NeurIPS2025 reviewers.** For detailed requirements, please refer to the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines).

croissant_file.description: If you checked the Dataset Submission box, upload a Croissant metadata file that documents your dataset. If your submission has more than one Croissant metadata file, please package all files into a single ZIP archive and upload it here. **Before uploading, verify that your file is valid using the [Croissant validator](https://huggingface.co/spaces/JoaquinVanschoren/croissant-checker).** If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this field empty.

dataset_URL.description: If you checked the Dataset Submission box, provide the URL to your dataset here. **Before including the URL for your dataset, verify that you followed the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines) (as part of the CFPs) and that the URL is accessible to NeurIPS2025 reviewers.** If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this field empty.

dataset_final_confirmation.description: **By checking this box, you confirm that: (1)** your dataset is complete and finalized at the time of submission; **(2)** you included a valid Croissant metadata file that has been verified using the [Croissant validator](https://huggingface.co/spaces/luisoala/croissant-checker); **(3)** you followed the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines); **(4)** you provided a URL pointing to the dataset that is accessible for NeurIPS2025 reviewers. If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this box unchecked.

checklist_confirmation.description: In order to improve the rigor and transparency of research submitted to and published at NeurIPS, authors are required to complete a paper checklist and include it in the paper PDF. See [https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist](https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist) and the provided 2025 sample LaTeX file. **Papers not including the checklist in the paper PDF will be desk rejected.**

enum.description: I confirm that I have included a paper checklist in the paper PDF.

code_URL.description: If your submission includes code, provide the URL to a hosting platform (e.g., Github, Bitbucket) as described in the CFPs. See the main track [code guidelines](https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for details.

supplementary_material.description: All supplementary material must be self-contained and zipped into a single file. Note that supplementary material will be visible to reviewers throughout and after the review period, and **ensure all your supplementary material is anonymized if your submission is anonymized.** The maximum file size is 100MB. Supplementary material can be updated until the supplementary material deadline (May 22).

financial_support.description: Optionally indicate one student author on the paper who would need financial support to attend and present at the conference if the paper is accepted (or leave blank if financial support is not needed). Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors.

reviewer_nomination.description: Every submission must nominate at least one author who is a qualified reviewer (i.e., satisfying our reviewer nomination criteria [https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/](https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/) ). Being named as such a reviewer in the submission constitutes an acceptance and a commitment to carry out the regular reviewing load (~6 papers) responsibly if asked by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).

responsible_reviewing.description: We acknowledge that every author on the program committee is obligated to conduct responsible reviewing according to the policy designed by the PC Chairs and relevant members of the organizing committee. **Failure to do so may result in desk rejection or other serious consequences.**

enum.description: We acknowledge the responsible reviewing obligations as authors.
